result.title: A six-month periodic fasting reduces microalbuminuria and improves metabolic control in patients with type 2 diabetes and diabetic nephropathy: a randomized controlled study

knowledge_units.context_summary: A randomized controlled study evaluated the effects of a six-month fasting-mimicking diet versus a Mediterranean diet on patients with type 2 diabetes and diabetic nephropathy. The intervention significantly reduced microalbuminuria and improved metabolic markers like HOMA-IR and suPAR in the fasting-mimicking group. However, these improvements were not sustained at the three-month follow-up, potentially due to a lack of change in dicarbonyl detoxification and DNA-damage markers.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study investigates the impact of a periodic fasting-mimicking diet on albumin-to-creatinine ratio and metabolic markers in patients with type 2 diabetes. It highlights the role of hyperglycemia, dicarbonyl stress, and DNA damage in diabetic kidney disease progression. The research design involves a randomized, controlled, open study at the University Hospital in Heidelberg, which includes specific inclusion criteria and monitoring protocols.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study utilized a stratified randomization procedure based on BMI and HbA1c to assign participants to either a fasting-mimicking diet or a Mediterranean diet. The intervention consisted of five consecutive days with specific dietary guidelines each month, during which the insulin dosage and oral antidiabetic medications were adjusted during the fasting period. Monitoring included self-reported blood sugar levels, blood pressure, and physical activity, with blood chemistry analysis performed at the University Hospital in Heidelberg.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study defined primary and secondary endpoints, including ACR changes and metabolic markers, and detailed the statistical methods and power calculations. A sample size of 40 was determined to detect a 30% reduction in ACR, with 38 patients completing three cycles and 33 completing the full study. Analysis was conducted on an intention-to-treat basis using ANCOVA and hierarchical testing in R.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study attributes participant withdrawal to Covid-19 pandemic restrictions and notes comparable baseline anthropometric and metabolic measures between groups. The fasting-mimicking diet (FMD) significantly reduced albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) in patients with microalbuminuria after three and six cycles, while showing no significant difference in the macroalbuminuria subgroup. FMD also improved urea levels, cystatin C-based eGFR, suPAR, and HbA1c compared to the Mediterranean diet, though fasting plasma glucose and lipid levels remained unchanged.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The fasting-mimicking diet group experienced significantly greater weight loss than the Mediterranean diet group over six cycles, though body composition remained unchanged. Responders to the diet showed distinct acetylcarnitine levels and lower baseline ACR, while metabolic improvements like HOMA-IR reduction were sustained at follow-up. No significant changes were observed in dicarbonyl stress markers or DNA damage indicators.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The fasting-mimicking diet was well tolerated with no severe adverse effects and comparable hypoglycemic rates to the Mediterranean diet. The intervention allowed for significant reductions in antihyperglycemic and antihypertensive medications in the FMD group, while the M-Diet group required medication increases. Blood ketones increased three-fold in the FMD group, while the M-Diet group maintained high compliance scores.

FMD-induced reductions in microalbuminuria were reversed after refeeding and did not affect patients with macroalbuminuria, unlike SGLT-2 inhibitors. Improved metabolic control was achieved through reduced medication requirements, though weight loss and glycemic control alone do not fully explain the antialbuminuric effect. Responders were distinguished by specific acylcarnitine and amino acid profiles, with glycine potentially offering renal protection.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study found that fasting-mimicking diet did not activate key dicarbonyl detoxification pathways or repair DNA damage, potentially explaining the rapid return of albuminuria after the intervention. The lack of change in methylglyoxal and hydroxyacetone suggests that metabolic shifts were more complex than simple caloric restriction. The study highlights the clinical importance of fasting in type 2 diabetes while noting limitations such as the isocaloric control diet and the need for longer intervention periods.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study acknowledges limitations including a small sample size and the absence of kidney biopsies to assess renal cell metabolism. It concludes that fasting-mimicking diet cycles can be integrated into clinical practice to reduce albuminuria and improve metabolic control in type 2 diabetes patients. The lack of change in dicarbonyl detoxification and DNA-damage markers suggests that longer intervention periods may be necessary to prevent albuminuria relapse.
